The Abyssal grenadier Coryphaenoides armatus is a dominant benthopelagic fish of the deep North Atlantic, where ambient temperatures remain stable near 3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C]. Studies of its reproductive biology suggest a maximum reproductive output of approximately 6,935 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 6,935 eggs per year], a rate inferred from oocyte counts and spawning frequency under these cold, stable conditions. This modest fecundity reflects the slow metabolic pace imposed by the deep-sea thermal regime, where all physiological processes are sharply attenuated. Females likely release their yolked eggs in repeated spawning bouts, building a lifetime total across many low-cost events rather than concentrating output into a single energetic pulse. Such batch spawning is common among macrourids and aligns with the presumed low food supply at abyssal depths. The reproductive output is tightly linked to the ambient temperature of 3.3 °C, as any deviation in thermal conditions would alter the rate of oocyte development and the timing of gamete release. This thermal coupling indicates that climate-driven shifts in deep-water temperature could have direct consequences for the population dynamics of this long-lived, slow-growing species.

Newly hatched individuals of Coryphaenoides armatus emerge from a pelagic egg estimated to have an egg diameter of 2.6 mm, yielding a hatchling wet weight of approximately 0.0092 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0092 grams]. This minute starting mass is characteristic of macrourid fishes that produce numerous small, yolk-rich eggs dispersed into the water column. The hatchling is a yolk-sac larva, entirely dependent on its endogenous reserves during the initial days following chorion rupture. The efficiency of yolk absorption and the timing of first exogenous feeding are critical to survival, as the slow development rates enforced by the cold deep-sea environment mean the larva must locate suitable prey before its nutritional reserves are exhausted. The low neonatal mass imposes a tight energetic budget: the larva must transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic feeding while growing rapidly enough to avoid prolonged vulnerability to the sparse suite of predators present in the mesopelagic zone. This initial mass sets the baseline for a lifetime growth trajectory that spans several decades and results in a very large ultimate body size.

As the fish progresses through its juvenile and sub-adult stages, it eventually attains sexual maturity, a milestone marked by the onset of gonadal recrudescence. At this transition, individuals typically measure approximately 40 centimeters [Lp = approximately 40 centimeters] in total length, a size that corresponds to a body mass of roughly 293 grams [Wwp = roughly 293 grams] based on the length-weight relationship derived for this species. Reaching puberty at this moderate size reflects a life-history strategy that balances the need for somatic growth against the advantages of early reproduction in a food-limited environment. The length at puberty represents about 40% of the ultimate total length, a proportion common among iteroparous deep-sea fishes that spread reproductive effort over many years. At this stage, the gonads begin vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, initiating the protracted spawning season typical of macrourids. The relatively late maturation, combined with the cold thermal regime of 3.3 °C, ensures that resources are directed first into reaching a body size large enough to support the energetic demands of repeated spawning events.

Adults of Coryphaenoides armatus can attain a maximum total length of 102 centimeters [Li = 102 centimeters], making it one of the larger species within its genus. At this ultimate size, the corresponding body mass reaches approximately 5,860 grams [Wwi = approximately 5,860 grams], a figure derived from the same length-weight allometry that described the size at puberty. This large adult mass represents a substantial accumulation of somatic tissue built up over a long growth period, during which the fish forages on benthic invertebrates and small fishes. The asymptotic length is approached gradually, with growth rates declining markedly after sexual maturity as energy is increasingly diverted toward reproduction. Reaching such a large size confers advantages in terms of fecundity, as larger females can accommodate more developing oocytes and spawn more frequently. The ultimate size also influences the species' role in the abyssal food web, as large individuals are likely less vulnerable to predation and can exploit a wider range of prey sizes. This large final mass is a striking feature of the species and underscores its position as a top benthopelagic predator in the deep sea.

The lifespan of Coryphaenoides armatus is estimated to be approximately 14,600 days [am = approximately 14,600 days] when maintained at the stable deep-sea temperature of 3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to roughly 40 years, is among the highest recorded for any macrourid fish and is consistent with the slow life-history pace typical of abyssal organisms. The extreme longevity is underpinned by the cold thermal environment, which depresses metabolic rates and slows the accumulation of cellular damage. Old individuals are believed to continue reproducing throughout most of their adult lives, contributing to a steady, low-level recruitment that sustains the population. The long lifespan also means that individuals accumulate considerable experience in locating food patches and avoiding the few predators present at depth, such as larger piscivorous fishes and sharks. Senescence in this species is likely gradual, with reproductive output declining only in the final years before death. This combination of very slow growth, late maturity, and exceptional longevity places Coryphaenoides armatus at the extreme slow end of the life-history continuum, a strategy well suited to the stable but resource-poor abyssal environment.
